Comment rendre justice à Joyce Echaquan: How Can Justice Be Done for Joyce Echaquan?
« Ma mère m’a légué une guerre, et sa vo: “My mother left me a war, and her voice to wage it, but what I really want today is my mommy’s smile”
Un foulard « Justice pour Joyce » est ac: A “Justice for Joyce” scarf hangs in front of the agora at the Joliette hospital.
« Ma mère m’a légué une guerre, et sa vo: “My mother left me a war, and her voice to wage it, but what I really want today is my mommy’s smile,” says the eldest daughter of Joyce Echaquan. The Atikamekw mother of seven died at the Centre hospitalier de Lanaudière, under a barrage of racist insults.
« Justice pour Joyce ! » s’exclamaient l: “Justice for Joyce!” her children cried out the day after her death last year. One year later, Joyce Echaquan’s family is still asking for justice. While the Manawan community wants to build bridges to prevent such a tragedy from happening again, it says it keeps running into walls.
<strong>« Il va y avoir un travail à fai: “There will be work to do to reach that forgiveness”
Carol Dubé, Diane Echaquan, Solange Dubé: Carol Dubé, Diane Echaquan, Solange Dubé and Marie-Wasianna Echaquan Dubé speak in front of the Joliette hospital, one year after Joyce Echaquan’s death. Photo: Julien Forest
Un an plus tard, jour pour jour, la fami: One year later, to the day, Joyce Echaquan’s family went to pay their respects in the room where she spent the last moments of her life. The wound is still raw for her husband, Carol Dubé. “Words cannot describe the state we have been in for the past few days.
This date is the saddest there could be. We must all remember what happened here, on this very date last year. We all saw the final moments of my dear wife, Joyce, on social media,” he said during the commemorative ceremony held in front of the Centre hospitalier de Lanaudière. The widower hopes his wife’s death will open the door to systemic change.
« La porte qu’elle a ouverte est trop im: “The door she opened is too important; she cannot have died in vain,” says Carol Dubé. He addresses the crowd gathered in front of the Joliette hospital. “I have seen voices rise up against systemic racism. We now have a common mission to change things. I hope that together we will find the strength we need. It seems so important to me that it was a woman, my Joyce, who gave us the courage to build a more just society. I am confident that with humility, we can move forward together on the path of healing and reconciliation.”
Marie-Wasianna Echaquan Dubé est arrivée: Marie-Wasianna Echaquan Dubé arrived at the hospital a few minutes after watching <l1>the Facebook video her mother filmed</l1> before her death. One year later, she speaks through the family’s spokesperson, Solange Dubé.
« Je n’ai pas envie de parler, j’aurais: “I don’t feel like talking, I feel like screaming. I wish I weren’t afraid, I wish the world would understand the pain I’m living through. The absence is so great, the emptiness so cruel, her end was so unjust. I don’t want to be here, I want to be with my family, I want my mother to still be with us, I want peace,” she says, as relayed by Solange Dubé.
Karine Echaquan chante une chanson pour: Karine Echaquan sings a song for her cousin, Joyce Echaquan, in front of the agora at the Joliette hospital. Photo: Lela Savic
<strong>Au-delà des insultes racistes, u: Beyond the racist insults, a system that kills
Si on a souvent montré du doigt l’infirm: While fingers have often been pointed at the nurse and the orderly who hurled the insults, Carol Dubé has said publicly many times that it was systemic racism that killed his wife. But how did systemic racism kill Joyce? “The video shows two minutes of what happened, but there are much broader and more important things to consider in this context,” says Patrick Martin-Ménard, the medical liability lawyer representing the patient’s family. For him, an entire system failed. He believes Joyce Echaquan’s symptoms, pain and complaints were never taken seriously by the medical staff.
« On lui a accolé une étiquette », expli: “A label was stuck on her,” explains Martin-Ménard. For several months, Ms. Echaquan had been suffering from severe stomach pain. Despite several consultations, she had not received a diagnosis. “They quickly ended up prescribing her narcotics and morphine to relieve the pain,” says the lawyer. This pattern continued over many visits. On the evening of September 27, after an ambulance ride of several hours, Ms. Echaquan was determined to find the cause of her pain. “She was quickly labelled a drug addict in withdrawal who was trying to get narcotics,” the lawyer says.
Le message circule parmi le personnel de: The message circulated among hospital staff and became distorted by the time it reached the care teams. “It was this information that determined how she was treated by the two people we hear in the video: the nurse and the orderly. It’s essentially based on prejudice.” During her fatal visit to the hospital, Ms. Echaquan suffered cardiac failure that ultimately led to her death, because staff at her bedside did not treat her.
Ses proches demandent que ces comporteme: Her loved ones are asking for these behaviours to stop and for the non-Indigenous population to be aware of the stereotypes it holds about Indigenous people. “Prejudice isn’t only the crude things the nurse and the orderly said in the video.
Il y a des choses beaucoup plus subtiles: There are much more subtle things, deeply rooted in people’s minds, that need to be deconstructed,” the lawyer believes. Martin-Ménard constantly hears stories of racism, contemptuous and condescending attitudes, and stereotypes directed at Indigenous and vulnerable people. “What Ms. Echaquan documented is one case among others.
Ce n’est pas un cas isolé, une pomme pou: It’s not an isolated case, a bad apple, one racist nurse in the system. It reflects a mentality and a way of doing things across the whole system,” he says. In his view, it is hard to tackle the problem while the government refuses to recognize systemic racism, a racism that persists in the health care system, to the point of having cost Joyce Echaquan her life.
<strong>Justice pour Joyce : qui protège: Justice for Joyce: who is being protected?
« L’avocat de l’infirmière qu’on entend: “The lawyer for the nurse we hear most in the video painted a picture of a dangerous Atikamekw community from which hospital staff needed to be protected. But the only person who was in danger, and who died, was Joyce,” says a close friend of the Echaquan Dubé family who prefers to remain anonymous. The family’s lawyer denounces the hospital’s lack of transparency. “What I find shocking from the family’s point of view is seeing that Ms. Echaquan’s entire medical file, very specific details of her private life, ended up in the public square and was reported in the media. On the hospital’s side, the witnesses get blanket protection,” Martin-Ménard points out.
La journée même de l’anniversaire de la: On the very anniversary of Joyce Echaquan’s death, the verdict came down for Paule Rocray, the nurse who hurled racist insults at the patient. She was barred from practising for one year after being found guilty on two counts. In Martin-Ménard’s eyes, it is a lenient sentence.
« On croit que le conseil disciplinaire: “We believe the disciplinary council could have gone much further and laid many more charges,” says the lawyer, who argues that only the bare minimum was done. Martin-Ménard also denounces the fact that the disciplinary council took nearly 10 months to lay charges. Furthermore, the Ordre des infirmières et des infirmiers du Québec (OIIQ) had not reported that a college-level candidate for the nursing practice exam (CEPI) was working in the emergency room and with Joyce Echaquan at the time of the events, something revealed by the coroner’s inquiry. “Ms. Echaquan was under the responsibility of a student, who should never have had an unstable patient under her care,” Martin-Ménard recalls, adding that he considers this one of the main causes of the patient’s death. “She did not detect the signs of heart failure that appeared in Ms. Echaquan. A video, filmed by her daughter Marie-Wasianna Echaquan Dubé, clearly shows Ms. Echaquan in cardiorespiratory arrest.
La CEPI est présente et lui dit que tout: The CEPI is there and tells her everything is fine. She says it’s only the medication taking effect.” Although justice is slow, the lawyer hopes the coroner’s report, which is still awaited, will not only shed light on the events but also lead to concrete solutions. “There certainly needs to be some reflection and changes made so there is a better balance between victims and defendants, and so that justice is accessible,” he says.
La sécurisation culturelle est prônée pa: Cultural safety is advocated by many Indigenous people as a way to correct these dangerous prejudices. Under the concept of cultural safety, Indigenous people have the right to receive health care delivered with respect for the patient’s identity. Could this approach be applied in Quebec’s health care system, starting with the hospital where Joyce lost her life? Asked about this, Pascale Lamy, director of institutional affairs and public relations at the Centre intégré de santé et de services sociaux de Lanaudière (CISSSLAN), says a public announcement organized with the chief of the Atikamekw community of Manawan, Mr. Paul-Émile Ottawa, will take place in early October. It will be an opportunity to address the issue.
« Vous aurez l’occasion d’entendre les a: “You will have the opportunity to hear about the actions that have been put in place over the past few months to foster a bond of trust between members of the Atikamekw community of Manawan and our organization,” we were told, without any specifics on the nature of those actions. For Hayley Morris, a manager at the Mohawk Council of Kahnawake, cultural safety in the health care system is a personal issue.
« Pour beaucoup d’autochtones, c’est vra: “For many Indigenous people, it’s really hard to go to a big hospital where they are misunderstood,” she says. The young woman considers herself lucky to have a hospital at the heart of her community, where she feels safe. At the Kateri Memorial Hospital, she is immediately reassured by the signs and posters written in Kanien’keha on the walls.
Elle n’a pas à s’inquiéter pour ses proc: She doesn’t have to worry about her loved ones. “It’s a modern hospital with state-of-the-art facilities, but I see my traditional culture there,” says the Mohawk Council of Kahnawake employee. “It makes me happy to feel represented and to know that this institution truly cares about my health.” Recently, her mother-in-law had to receive health care far from home. “She went to a hospital outside our community and was treated in an atrocious way,” says an indignant Morris.
Elle raconte que le personnel de l’hôpit: She says hospital staff refused to grant simple requests. “There were nurses who wouldn’t even look at her or talk to her. The only one who was open to offering her help was a racialized nurse,” the young woman says. According to her, the problem lies in the lack of dialogue between Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities. She also points to the comments made by the care staff toward Ms. Echaquan.
« Je crois vraiment qu’ils pensent comme: “I truly believe they think that way because of a lack of interaction with Indigenous people,” she says. A first step, in her view, would be to offer training that raises care staff’s awareness of Indigenous realities.
« Nous avons des enjeux de santé qui déc: “We have health issues that stem from alcoholism, trauma and colonialism. If care staff are better informed about these realities, they will have greater empathy for their Indigenous patients,” she says. Morris also suggests that Indigenous Elders help raise hospital staff’s awareness of the realities of their communities. She would also like to see more health resources allocated to Indigenous communities, having witnessed the benefits such initiatives can bring. A graduate of Concordia University, she has fond memories of the Otsenhákta Student Centre, which offers services to Indigenous students. “There was an Elder you could consult and a room dedicated to traditional medicine,” she recalls. “It was reassuring for me to be among my own people.” Morris is constantly educating people about Indigenous realities and culture. She believes institutions also have a part to play in facilitating this dialogue, as does the non-Indigenous population.
« Les autochtones ne peuvent pas porter: “Indigenous people cannot carry the burden of raising awareness all by themselves,” she says. Barbara Flamand was a cultural safety liaison officer for the Manawan community at the Joliette hospital. She was on site when Joyce Echaquan died under the racist insults of the medical staff. No one told her Joyce Echaquan was in the health care facility. It was only when the victim’s mother, Diane Echaquan, called to tell her that her daughter was asking for help in a video on Facebook that she went to the emergency room.
Mais il était trop tard lorsqu’elle est: But it was too late by the time she arrived. After an hour’s wait in the emergency room, she was told the patient had died. One year later, the former liaison officer says she still doesn’t know why she wasn’t called. She believes Joyce Echaquan would not have died had she been there. “I withdrew into myself for a year, I resigned. I blame myself,” she says, unable to hold back her tears at the commemoration ceremony.
Aujourd’hui, la famille de Joyce Echaqua: Today, Joyce Echaquan’s family wants the non-Indigenous population to be aware of the stereotypes that lead Indigenous people to be seen as dangerous, and of the harm these prejudices cause.
La sénatrice innue Michèle Audette croit: Innu Senator Michèle Audette also believes there is still a great deal of awareness-raising work to be done. A former commissioner of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, Audette denounces the way the media feed the stereotype of the dangerous Indigenous person, notably in the case of Cindy Gladue, another Indigenous woman who died in tragic circumstances. “In the media, this Indigenous woman is never named; she is described as a prostitute, a sex worker, an Indian, while the person who committed the crime against her is named.
C’est un gros problème », souligne l’anc: It’s a big problem,” stresses the former president of Quebec Native Women. In her view, it is this kind of discourse that feeds the problem.
« On finit par normaliser la violence co: “We end up normalizing violence against Indigenous women,” the senator says. Audette is nonetheless optimistic. Joyce Echaquan’s death sparked a public conversation, something she did not see 10 years ago. She hopes this momentum will continue and that Indigenous people will be able to take their rightful place in every sphere of society. “The media must dare to cover Indigenous issues to make us known to the general public,” she says. “If the government passes a bill, non-Indigenous citizens need to question its impact on Indigenous nations.”
<strong>Le combat pour faire reconnaître: The fight to have systemic racism and Joyce’s Principle recognized
«On a parlé de créer des ponts, et je pe: “We talked about building bridges, and I think the bridges were there, but walls were built on top of those bridges,” says Constant Awashish, Grand Chief of the Atikamekw Nation Council. Photo: Julien Forest
Pour rendre justice à la mère de famille: To do justice to the mother of seven, the Atikamekw community is asking the government to recognize systemic racism, a difficult fight according to Constant Awashish, Grand Chief of the Atikamekw Nation Council. “We’re talking about systemic racism, something that is hard to explain, and often hard to defend. But Joyce brought about a collective awakening. She showed the general public that inadequate treatment of First Nations people truly does exist.
C’est ce qu’elle a su représenter, c’est: That is what she was able to represent, what she was able to demonstrate as a woman. We owe her a great deal for the future of our children,” says the Grand Chief. “Every time I think of Joyce, I think of her children, of future generations. I think the work she began was to open the door to a collective awareness, among our people as well as among non-Indigenous people. That’s what we want. We talked about building bridges, and I think the bridges were there, but walls were built on top of those bridges.
Maintenant, il faut juste briser ces mur: Now, we just have to break down those walls, the walls of ignorance, the walls of hatred, the walls of fear of one another – that is what feeds our separation,” he adds. He believes more education about Indigenous realities is needed. The Atikamekw Grand Chief also asks the Quebec government “to compromise,” to revisit its position on systemic racism and to make September 28 a national day of commemoration in honour of Joyce Echaquan.
Les proches de Mme Echaquan souhaitent e: Ms. Echaquan’s loved ones also want the provincial government to adopt Joyce’s Principle, a demand reiterated by the Atikamekw community on September 28. It is tied to a brief submitted by the Atikamekw Council of Manawan and the Atikamekw Nation Council last November. The brief defends the rights of Indigenous people in Quebec and Canada in health and social services. Presented to the federal and provincial governments, “Joyce’s Principle aims to guarantee to all Indigenous people the right of equitable access, without any discrimination, to all social and health services, as well as the right to enjoy the best possible state of physical, mental, emotional and spiritual health.” It also requires “the recognition and respect” of traditional medicines. “I hope the governments of Quebec and Canada will adopt Joyce’s Principle so that this terrible event will not have happened in vain, so that her voice marks the beginning of real change for all Indigenous people, so that no one is ever again a victim of systemic racism,” Carol Dubé writes at the start of the brief. At the federal level, the Liberal Party said during the campaign that it will fully implement Joyce’s Principle. In Quebec, the CAQ announced earlier this year that it did not intend to adopt the Principle.
Le mardi 28 septembre, en session parlem: On Tuesday, September 28, during a session of the National Assembly, the premier said he agreed with the foundations of Joyce’s Principle. However, he said he was reluctant to adopt it because of the systemic racism it refers to. François Legault’s party rejected a motion on cultural safety for Indigenous people put forward by the opposition parties. As for the question of systemic racism, ministers Geneviève Guilbault and Ian Lafrenière refused to answer media questions on Tuesday, during the commemoration.
Le Salon bleu a également été le théâtre: The Blue Room (Salon bleu) was also the scene of a partisan clash over the issue. Disappointed by the Legault government’s lack of commitment, Indigenous chiefs are now turning to Quebecers to commit to ending the systemic racism that killed Joyce Echaquan.
